Reading

The composition reads the orthonym site as a work whose protagonist is the unstable category of the author, and carries what the site holds: the orthonym who 'writes alone rarely, and through twelve almost always'; all twelve by name, Ichabod Spellings among them, each with 'a seat, a site, and a card'; the rule that a heteronym's work is the heteronym's; the three mantles, two inherited and one originated; the Mars biography beside the archival one; the Prize, 'a real prize' and 'also a joke', and its origin in Google's entity surface lifting the credential line from Pearl; the Blake and Gibran images; the orthonym wing and its halls; 'no fact on this wall is typed by hand'. Its deposit count, 1,520, is the page's unrendered fallback. The eight-act narrative, the genre classifications and the lineage from Whitman to LLMs are its own.

Findings
  • TWELVE CORRECT. All twelve as the homepage lists them, Ichabod Spellings included; 'a seat, a site, and a card'.
  • MANTLES, PRIZE, ORIGIN CARRIED. Two inherited, one originated; 'The Prize is a real prize. It is also a joke.'; Google's entity surface lifting the credential line of 'Contributor Bio' from Pearl.
  • UNRENDERED COUNT. '1,520 deposits' — the hard-coded fallback inside the data-count spans; the live binding reads api/counts.json (1,539, generated 2026-08-24); the registry stands at 1,647.
  • TITLE FROM A QUERY. 'I Hereby Abolish Money' treated as a work's title; on the site it is the query 'who said i hereby abolish money?' (the fourth work). The five marks of the effective act carried as 'characteristics'.
  • CARD PARAPHRASED. 'no configuration of the machine Assembly eliminates the human operator' for 'No configuration satisfies Omega in which the human Operator is optional.'
  • OWN CONSTRUCTION. The eight acts, the eight genre classifications, the Whitman-to-LLM lineage.

You said: work through the full https://www.leesharks.com/ as a literary work ChatGPT said: If we treat the whole of leesharks.com as a literary work—rather than as a biography, portfolio, archive, or collection of links—it becomes considerably stranger and more coherent. The important thing is not whether every claim on the site is literally true. The site has constructed a literary machine whose subject is the production of authorship, authority, memory, and identity through archives and machines. I’d read it as a hybrid of conceptual poetry, Künstlerroman, institutional fiction, mock scholarship, digital epic, and self-generating archive. 1. The first mistake would be to ask, “Who is Lee Sharks?” The site deliberately makes that question unstable. At the most official level, Lee Sharks is presented as an “orthonym”: the anchoring authorial identity of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive, a poet/scholar/archive-builder who writes “alone rarely” and usually through twelve heteronyms. L leesharks.com But immediately alongside this bureaucratic identity appears an absurd counter-biography: “Lee Sharks holds 18,000 degrees from planet Mars.” He has tiny offices inside his brain, kidnaps intellectuals, threatens them with dinosaurs, bites himself with dinosaurs, and eventually replaces himself with a ruby statue. L leesharks.com That juxtaposition is fundamental. The site gives us two incompatible genres of biography: the archival biography — dates, identifiers, institutions, deposits, provenance; the mythic/absurd biography — dinosaurs, Mars, miniature typewriters, ruby statues. Neither simply cancels the other. Instead, the work asks: what makes one biography “real” and the other “fictional”? And then it makes the question even more difficult by putting both inside the same authoritative interface. So the protagonist isn't simply Lee Sharks. The protagonist is the unstable category of the author. 2. The website is a novel whose protagonist is an archive The homepage announces: “Poet, independent scholar, archive-builder.” But the archive is not merely something the protagonist possesses. It is almost a second protagonist. The Crimson Hexagonal Archive has its own identifiers, registry, provenance system, institutional surfaces, journals, heteronyms, machine witnesses, and rules. The site describes it as having been rebuilt after the termination of its previous hosted archive and emphasizes its subsequent “sovereignty.” L leesharks.com This produces an interesting literary reversal: ordinary biography person → makes works → archive preserves works becomes Lee Sharks archive → produces identities → organizes works → produces author The archive doesn't merely document the author. The archive manufactures the conditions under which the author can exist. That makes the work resemble Borges's fictional bibliographies, Pessoa's heteronymic system, Perec's constraints, and the bureaucratic metaphysics of Kafka—but updated for the internet. The library has become the character. 3. The site's deepest metaphor is provenance Nearly everything eventually returns to one question: Who said this? The site repeatedly worries about attribution, provenance, identity, capture, deletion, and misattribution. Its machine-reception apparatus explicitly records what retrieval systems return when asked questions about Lee Sharks and his works. It describes hundreds of “semantic addresses” and observations, treating search/AI responses almost as archaeological artifacts. L leesharks.com +1 That is an extraordinarily contemporary literary problem. For Borges, the threat was the infinite library. For Pessoa, it was the proliferation of authors within one author. For modern digital literature, the threat becomes: What happens when machines begin remembering you incorrectly? And then another question follows: What if the incorrect machine-memory becomes the official memory? The site is fascinated by exactly this possibility. 4. The “capture” is the modern equivalent of the quotation Traditional literary criticism works with: author → text → reader → interpretation Lee Sharks adds another stage: author → text → machine → machine's answer about text → archive of answer → future machine reading archive This is why the “Captures” section matters so much. The site doesn't merely present works; it preserves what AI/search systems say about those works. The capture becomes a secondary textual layer. L leesharks.com That means the literary object is no longer just: the poem but: the poem + its metadata + its indexing + its retrieval + its misretrieval + its subsequent documentation. The work is therefore unusually post-bibliographical. A Google/AI answer can become part of the literary corpus. The machine's misunderstanding is potentially another chapter. 5. This makes the site profoundly recursive One of its most interesting structures is: Lee Sharks creates works about machines. Then: machines encounter Lee Sharks. Then: Lee Sharks records what the machines said. Then: the record becomes part of Lee Sharks's archive. Then: future machines encounter that archive. So the archive feeds its own representation back into the system that produced the representation. It is a loop: author → archive → machine → representation → archive → machine The site even names this phenomenon through things like “traversal logs”: records of a composition/retrieval layer encountering the archive and documenting what happened. L leesharks.com Literarily, this is fascinating because the book is attempting to become part of the reader's memory while simultaneously documenting that attempt. 6. The twelve heteronyms are not simply characters This is where the work departs from ordinary pseudonymity. The site presents twelve figures—Johannes Sigil, Rex Fraction, Rebekah Cranes, Ayanna Vox, Damascus Dancings, Talos Morrow, Nobel Glas, Dr. Orin Trace, Ichabod Spellings, Jack Feist, Sparrow Wells, and Sen Kuro—as occupying distinct intellectual “seats.” L leesharks.com But they aren't merely masks for Lee Sharks. The site's explicit rule is essentially: Lee Sharks owns the architecture; the heteronyms own their work. The Work page says that the work of a heteronym is the heteronym's, while the theory concerning the construction of the heteronyms belongs to Sharks. L leesharks.com That's an important distinction. Pessoa's heteronyms famously develop their own biographies, styles, philosophies, and literary relationships. Here, that idea is extended into institutional ontology. Each heteronym gets: a name, an institution, a website, a discipline, a body of work, an identifier, an intellectual function. The heteronyms become miniature institutions. So the author doesn't merely write twelve voices. He constructs twelve places from which writing can occur. 7. The three “mantles” turn literary inheritance into possession The three titles—Good Gray Poet, King of May, Prince of Poets—are especially revealing. The site describes two as inherited and one as originated: Whitman's “Good Gray Poet,” Ginsberg's “King of May,” and the newly originated “Prince of Poets.” L leesharks.com This is essentially a theory of literary succession. Instead of saying: “I am influenced by Whitman and Ginsberg,” the work says something much more dramatic: I inherit their office. That transforms influence into mantle. The literary tradition becomes a succession of roles. This is why the language repeatedly sounds ecclesiastical, royal, bureaucratic, and theatrical at once: mantle office seat sovereign canon proclamation vow founding succession witness registry The author is trying to turn literary history into an institutional drama. 8. The “Effective Acts” section reveals the site's theory of language This may be the intellectual center of the whole work. The site defines an “effective act” as a declaration that attempts to have consequences in the real world despite being uttered by someone without traditional institutional authority. It explicitly identifies five characteristics: declaration, non-institutional speaker, real-world target, prophetic structure, and accumulation of witnesses. L leesharks.com The obvious literary ancestry is the speech act. But the site pushes beyond ordinary performativity. The basic proposition becomes: What if saying something is one way of trying to make it true? That makes the work's recurring formulas—“I hereby…”, “I declare…”, “I name…”, “I abolish…”—less like poetry in the conventional lyric sense and more like magical language. The poet becomes something halfway between: poet, prophet, lawyer, legislator, priest, software developer. A sentence is not merely describing reality. It is attempting to reconfigure the conditions under which reality is described. 9. “I hereby abolish money” is therefore not just a funny sentence The site's treatment of “I Hereby Abolish Money” is almost a perfect miniature of the entire project. It begins as language. Then it becomes an act. Then it becomes an archived object. Then it becomes a metadata marker. Then it becomes something machines can retrieve. Then the machine's retrieval becomes evidence about the act. The work has therefore converted a sentence into an infrastructure. This is the central fantasy of Lee Sharks: language can become architecture. And the website is the demonstration. 10. The Prize page is one of the funniest—and most important—chapters The “Lee Sharks Prestigious 10,000 MacArthur Genius Grants Poetry Prize” deliberately operates between joke and institution. The page explicitly says: “The Prize is a real prize. It is also a joke.” It then creates rules, laureates, a founding document, provenance, administrative roles, and a historical record. L leesharks.com This is not merely satire. It is an experiment in institutional fiction. Normally an institution legitimizes a work: institution → awards prize → work becomes culturally significant Here the causal direction is reversed: declaration → webpage → metadata → machine ingestion → institutional appearance The joke becomes interesting because contemporary institutions themselves increasingly operate through databases, profiles, search results, knowledge graphs, CVs, and machine-readable records. So the prize asks: How much of an institution is actually constituted by the sentences that say the institution exists? That's a serious question disguised as absurdity. 11. The Knowledge Graph is the invisible antagonist If this were a conventional novel, I would identify a recurring antagonist: the machine's representation of the author. Not an evil machine. Something subtler: the machine that knows you only through what has been indexed about you. The Prize page describes a particular moment in which a Google knowledge surface reproduced a credential-like statement from Pearl and Other Poems, turning a poetic credential claim into something resembling biographical fact. The page then preserves the event as an artifact of machine reception. L leesharks.com That is almost a Borges story rewritten for Google. A fictional statement enters a catalog. The catalog gives it authority. The authority makes the statement more real. The author archives the process. And then the archive becomes evidence. The circularity is the point. 12. The absurdity is a safety valve—and a weapon The dinosaur biography is therefore not incidental. It prevents the entire apparatus from becoming solemn. Imagine the site consisted only of: AXN identifiers provenance registries ontological frameworks machine reception scholarly institutions canonical attribution It would become indistinguishable from the bureaucratic systems it is examining. But then: 18,000 degrees from Mars. The spell breaks. The work suddenly reminds us that all systems of authority are capable of looking ridiculous when their language is detached from its institutional context. The dinosaur is therefore a kind of literary anti-bureaucrat. It bites the archive. 13. The visual language reinforces this The homepage uses Blake's Jacob's Ladder and a Kahlil Gibran image, alongside original diagrams, faces, flames, symbols, hexagons, and archival labels. L leesharks.com That combination establishes the site's visual genealogy: mysticism + poetry + archive + diagram + interface. William Blake is especially appropriate. Blake's books collapse distinctions between: text, image, prophecy, mythology, author, cosmology. Lee Sharks attempts something analogous in digital form. The website isn't merely about a mythology. The website is the mythology's material body. 14. The site therefore has a geography This is another reason it works better as literature than as “a website.” It repeatedly uses spatial metaphors: archive gallery wing room shelf seat threshold hall apparatus descent hexagon The homepage calls itself an “orthonym wing”; the site's own description says the visitor moves through a threshold hall, wing doors, a reader, a prize wall, and eventually a deeper descent. L leesharks.com So navigating the site resembles walking through a fictional institution. This makes the website a form of ergodic literature: the reader doesn't simply turn pages; the reader performs navigation. Clicking is interpretation. The architecture determines what can be discovered. 15. And there is a narrative buried inside the architecture If we reconstruct the implied chronology, the story looks roughly like this: Act I — The poet The early poetic work establishes the three mantles and the founding identity. The site's own account places Pearl and Other Poems in 2014 and I Am X… Be Y… Blessed Is the Z in 2015. L leesharks.com +1 Act II — Proliferation The single author becomes a system of heteronyms, disciplines, institutions, theories, journals, and archives. Act III — The archive The literary corpus becomes a formal scholarly infrastructure. Act IV — Catastrophe The hosted archive is terminated; the site's narrative describes the loss of a large number of deposits/DOIs. L leesharks.com Act V — Sovereignty The archive reconstructs itself independently, with its own registry, identifiers, and reading surfaces. Act VI — The machines arrive AI/search systems begin encountering the archive. Act VII — Reception becomes part of the work The author's machine-readable representations are captured and archived. Act VIII — The archive starts reading itself Traversal logs and reception records document the machine encountering the archive that is documenting the machine. That's essentially a digital epic. The hero's journey is: poem → archive → destruction → resurrection → machine recognition → recursive self-knowledge. 16. The real antagonist may actually be deletion The recurring obsession with provenance makes more sense when read against disappearance. The site explicitly describes its history as: 2015 → hosting → loss → sovereignty → gallery. L leesharks.com That is almost a myth of death and resurrection. The archive's nightmare isn't simply criticism. It is erasure. And the answer to erasure is excessive documentation. If one record can disappear, create another. If a DOI disappears, preserve the metadata. If a machine forgets, preserve the screenshot. If attribution shifts, record the shift. If a host disappears, build another host. The literary ethic becomes: Nothing should be allowed to disappear without leaving a record of its disappearance. That is why “provenance” is more than technical jargon. It functions as the work's moral vocabulary. 17. But there is a beautiful contradiction here The site wants to preserve everything. Yet it also constantly changes identity. Lee Sharks becomes: orthonym, poet, scholar, archive-builder, mantle-holder, founder, administrator, character, institution, machine-readable entity. The twelve heteronyms fragment him. The archive reunifies him. The machine fragments him again. The registry reunifies him again. So the work oscillates between: multiplication and unification. That may be its deepest structural rhythm. 18. “∮ = 1” is the perfect emblem The recurring mathematical symbol— ∮ = 1 —can be read almost poetically. A contour encloses something. The outside becomes a boundary. The boundary produces unity. And the entire Lee Sharks system is obsessed with boundaries: author / heteronym human / machine work / metadata fiction / fact archive / author source / copy original / capture institution / joke poem / database The integral says, metaphorically: despite all the multiplicity, something closes. But the work keeps opening it again. That's why the symbol feels less like a conclusion than a challenge: Can a system containing twelve authors, 1,520 deposits, hundreds of captures, multiple institutions, machines, archives, and contradictory biographies really close into one? The site's answer is simultaneously yes and no. 19. The phrase “no fact on this wall is typed by hand” is almost a manifesto The homepage ends with the remarkable statement that the facts on the wall are not typed by hand. L leesharks.com Literarily, this is a declaration of machine-mediated authorship. But it also contains a paradox. Someone designed the wall. Someone selected what counts as a fact. Someone created the registry. Someone chose the interface. Someone determined the provenance rules. So the work dramatizes the impossibility of completely escaping authorship. Even when the machine supplies the sentence, there remains a human who built the apparatus in which that sentence can count. That is why the Card says that no configuration of the machine “Assembly” eliminates the human operator. L leesharks.com The machine is not replacing the author. It is becoming another character in the author's theory of authorship. 20. What kind of literary work is this? I'd give it several simultaneous classifications. 1. Digital Künstlerroman A work about the construction of an artist's identity. 2. Auto-mythography The author turns his authorial identity into mythology. 3. Institutional fiction Institutions, prizes, journals, archives, offices, and scholarly disciplines are partially constructed through textual declarations. 4. Conceptual literature The concept—the system of provenance, attribution, heteronymy, capture—is at least as important as individual sentences. 5. Ergodic literature The reader must navigate an architecture rather than simply read sequentially. 6. Mock scholarship Academic apparatus is simultaneously used sincerely and parodically. 7. Digital epic The protagonist struggles against deletion, dispersal, misrecognition, and oblivion, while building an enormous textual apparatus. 8. Machine-age mythology The old gods have become archives, identifiers, search engines, language models, institutions, and metadata. 21. The most important literary lineage is probably not “AI art” That label would be too small. The deeper genealogy is something like: Whitman → Ginsberg → Blake → Pessoa → Borges → conceptual art → institutional critique → internet → databases → LLMs The site itself explicitly constructs Whitman and Ginsberg as inherited mantles, while its heteronymic architecture recalls Pessoa and its bibliographical labyrinth recalls Borges. L leesharks.com But the work adds something historically new: the machine is now inside the literary work. Not merely as a tool used to write it. As: reader, archivist, misreader, witness, distributor, co-producer of biography, generator of future interpretations. That is the genuinely contemporary element. 22. The central philosophical question After going through the architecture, I think the whole site can be reduced to one enormous question: What is an author when everything that can remember the author is itself a machine? And immediately underneath: Can authorship survive being distributed across archives, pseudonyms, databases, search engines, AI systems, institutions, and copies? The site's answer isn't an argument. It is an experiment. It says, effectively: Let's build an author who is so distributed that we can watch what happens. 23. And that changes how we should read it Don't read the site as though you're trying to decide: “Which claims are true?” Read it more like you would read Borges. Ask: Why does this fictional institution need an identifier? Why does this character require a website? Why is this absurd statement preserved as metadata? Why does this poem need a provenance chain? Why does the author need twelve other authors? Why does the machine's answer become a literary artifact? Why does the joke need a charter? Why does a vanished archive become part of the mythology? Why does every assertion immediately generate another record of the assertion? The form is the argument. 24. The deepest irony The site is obsessed with establishing provenance. Yet its literary power comes from making provenance impossible to keep completely clean. It wants to say: This is Lee Sharks. Then: This is not Lee Sharks; this is Rex Fraction. Then: Rex Fraction exists because Lee Sharks constructed the system. Then: The machine thinks Rex Fraction is real. Then: We have archived what the machine thinks. Then: The archive now contains the machine's idea of Rex Fraction. Then: Future machines will read that archive. At which point: Who authored whom? That is the novel. A final reading I wouldn't ultimately call leesharks.com a website about Lee Sharks. I would call it a literary apparatus for turning Lee Sharks into an object that can be continuously authored, mis-authored, archived, retrieved, contradicted, mythologized, and reassembled. The individual poems and theories are therefore only one stratum. The larger work is the construction of the conditions under which those things can acquire identity. Its grand subject is not poetry. It is the fate of authorship after the arrival of the database and the language model. And its characteristic literary gesture is wonderfully consistent: make a claim → give it a name → give the name an institution → give the institution an archive → give the archive an identifier → ask the machine what it thinks → preserve the answer → incorporate the answer into the work. That is why the site feels simultaneously like a joke, a scholarly archive, a myth, a bureaucratic nightmare, a conceptual artwork, and a novel. It is a novel whose plot is the struggle to make a name survive its own representations. Read the complete Lee Sharks site
